title: What a global platform work standard would mean for India
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Three scenarios for delivery partners, drivers and home-service workers.
body:
In mid-June 2026 the International Labour Conference in Geneva reached the end of its discussion on platform work. The original version of this post was written while the Conference was in session, and it set out three ways the outcome could go: a binding convention, a recommendation only, or a delay. The Conference has since closed, so this version keeps the three scenarios as a way of thinking and then explains what actually happened, what the new standard says, how it compares with Indian law, and what India and its workers can do next. For delivery partners, ride-hailing drivers and home-service workers, the questions are very practical: who decides when an account is switched off, how is pay calculated, and what happens after an accident?

## What happened in Geneva

The 114th session of the Conference ran from 1 to 12 June 2026 and closed on 12 June by adopting the **Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy, 2026**, numbered **Convention No. 193**. It is the first international labour standard aimed at digital labour platforms. The vote, as reported by Human Rights Watch, was 406 in favour, 8 against and 36 abstentions, with the United States and New Zealand among those against. A more detailed, non-binding recommendation that was meant to accompany the convention was not finalised for lack of time, and the Conference only suggested that the ILO's Governing Body consider putting it on a future agenda. So of the three scenarios, the first one came true, with a partial echo of the third: a convention was adopted, but the guidance that would have helped to apply it is still to come.

## What the convention says

The text is long and technical, but its main features can be summarised in plain language.

- **Wide coverage.** It applies to digital labour platforms and to platform workers in both the formal and informal economies, whether they work in person, as taxi or delivery workers do, or online, as data labellers do. A country may exclude limited categories only after consulting employers and workers, and it must explain exclusions and extend coverage step by step where practicable.
- **Basic rights for everyone.** Whatever a worker's status under national law, the convention asks States to respect and promote freedom of association and collective bargaining, freedom from forced and child labour, protection against discrimination and a safe and healthy working environment. It also extends protection against violence and harassment to online and third-party abuse.
- **Correct classification.** States must take steps to ensure that workers are classified correctly, based mainly on how the work is actually done and paid for, and not on the platform's label of "independent contractor". The convention does not create a presumption of employment, but a State may adopt one.
- **Pay and information.** Workers must receive what they are due, subject only to lawful deductions, and clear and timely information about pay and deductions. For those in an employment relationship, rules such as the minimum wage and reimbursement of work-related expenses apply under national law; for others, States are asked to consider whether to extend such protections.
- **Social security.** Workers are to have access to social security on terms no less favourable than those for other workers of the same status.
- **Algorithmic management.** Platforms must disclose the automated systems they use to monitor, evaluate or make decisions about work and how those systems affect pay or access to work. Where an automated decision significantly harms a worker, for example by stopping payment, suspending or deactivating an account, the worker may ask for a written explanation and a review with meaningful human involvement. Suspension, deactivation or termination on discriminatory or otherwise unlawful grounds is prohibited.
- **Data and privacy.** Workers' personal data and privacy are to be protected.
- **Migrant workers.** Governments must guard against abuse during the recruitment and engagement of migrant and refugee platform workers.

Commentators have pointed out limits. Human Rights Watch notes that the minimum wage provisions apply directly only to employees and that tips are excluded, and that some workers may remain outside an employment relationship even when classification rules are correctly applied. The cross-border enforcement of the convention is left open.

## India's position

India's delegation to the Conference divided. According to a LiveLaw commentary, the Government delegate abstained, while the employers' delegate and the workers' delegate both voted in favour. No official explanation has been given for the abstention. The practical consequence is that India will not ratify the convention for now. An abstention is not a final position, since a country can ratify later, and the convention takes legal effect for a country only when it ratifies. Whether and when India does so will depend on a national discussion among the Government, employers and workers.

BMS's representative told the Conference in Geneva that fair treatment should extend to platform and gig workers, and welcomed the steps India and some States had already taken. The BRICS Trade Union Forum, hosted by BMS in Hyderabad in July, later welcomed the convention in its declaration and called on member countries to align national laws quickly so that platform workers are guaranteed collective bargaining and social protection.

## How Indian law compares

The Code on Social Security, 2020, in force since 21 November 2025, already gives India a base. It defines gig workers and platform workers, requires aggregators to contribute between 1 and 2 per cent of annual turnover to a Social Security Fund, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to such workers, and provides for registration on the e-Shram portal with a portable, Aadhaar-linked identity and notified benefits such as accident insurance, health and maternity cover. That matches the convention's emphasis on social security.

There are gaps in other areas, according to commentators. The Code does not treat gig and platform workers as employees and has no test for classification that looks at the facts of the relationship. It says little on algorithmic transparency, human review of deactivation or collective bargaining for platform workers. Those are the areas where the convention would ask more of India than current law does.

## What can be done now

Whether or not India ratifies, it can move ahead on matters that are within its power and that workers need today.

- **Finish rules and schemes** under the Social Security Code, so that the benefits promised on paper are actually available.
- **Register platform workers on e-Shram**, with simple procedures and help desks, because a worker who is not registered cannot claim anything.
- **Insist on aggregator contributions** and publish how the Fund is collected and spent.
- **Create a fair deactivation procedure**, with notice, reasons, a chance to respond and a human decision-maker, whether through rules, a code of conduct or State laws.
- **Make pay and deductions transparent**, so that a rider or driver can see how each payment was calculated.

Several State governments have also taken their own steps for gig workers, and their experience will be useful when national rules are written.

## For readers

The authoritative text of the convention is on the ILO website, and nothing in this post replaces it. Check the exact wording of any clause before relying on it, because the words that decide a right, such as whether a State "shall" act or "shall consider" acting, are in the details.
